title: Pullback — Interaktive Visualisierung

For differential forms, the pullback f*(ω) is defined so that the diagram commutes: evaluating f*(ω) on tangent vectors at p equals evaluating ω on the pushed-forward vectors at f(p).
The pullback is contravariant: a map going M -> N induces a map going 'the other way' on forms (N^* -> M^*), reversing the direction of the original map.
The pullback is the universal construction: any map from M to the 'function space' of N factors uniquely through f*, which is why it appears throughout differential geometry.
Pullbacks preserve algebraic structure: f*(g1 ∧ g2) = f*(g1) ∧ f*(g2) and f*(d g) = d(f* g), making them compatible with the exterior calculus.

title: Christoffel Symbols — Visual Explorer

thesis: An interactive English-language explorer that lets the user deform a 2D surface and watch the Christoffel symbols Γᵏᵢⱼ update in real time, showing how they measure the failure of the coordinate basis to be parallel, and how they enter the covariant derivative of a vector field on the surface.
key_claims: Christoffel symbols are the components of the Levi-Civita connection in a coordinate basis; they are determined entirely by the metric tensor and its first derivatives: Γᵏᵢⱼ = ½ gᵏˡ (∂ᵢ gⱡˡ + ∂ⱼ gᵢˡ − ∂ˡ gᵢⱼ).

On a flat surface in Cartesian coordinates all Christoffel symbols vanish, but on the same flat surface in polar coordinates they are nonzero — curvature is not the same as nonzero Christoffel symbols.
The covariant derivative ∇ᵢ Vʲ = ∂ᵢ Vʲ + Γʲᵢₖ Vᵏ corrects the ordinary derivative by subtracting the change in the basis vectors, giving a geometrically meaningful derivative on curved spaces.

Geodesic equations ẍᵏ + Γᵏᵢⱼ ẋⁱ ẋʲ = 0 are second-order ODEs whose solutions are the 'straightest possible' curves on the surface; Christoffel symbols act as the 'force' bending the coordinate trajectory.
Symmetry Γᵏᵢⱼ = Γᵏⱼᵢ (torsion-free) is a property of the Levi-Civita connection, not of arbitrary connections.

title: Fiber Bundles Lab

thesis: An interactive English-language lab that builds intuition for fiber bundles from the ground up: what a total space, base, and fiber are, how a connection (gauge field) lets you compare fibers at different base points (parallel transport), and how curvature measures the failure of parallel transport to be path-independent — with 3D renderings of common examples (trivial bundle, Möbius strip, SU(2) bundle).
key_claims: A fiber bundle is a surjection π: E -> B such that every point in B has a neighborhood whose preimage looks like U × F (local triviality); the 'fiber' F is the space you get by looking straight down at a base point.

A connection on a principal G-bundle is a choice of 'horizontal direction' at each point of E, equivalent to a Lie-algebra-valued 1-form ω satisfying equivariance and reproducing the fundamental vertical vectors; in physics this is the gauge potential A.
Parallel transport along a path γ in the base lifts γ to a horizontal path in E; the endpoint depends on the path if and only if the curvature F = dω + ½[ω,ω] is nonzero.

Holonomy: transporting a vector around a closed loop in the base and comparing it to the original gives an element of the structure group G; the collection of all holonomies is the holonomy group, which (by Ambrose-Singer) is generated by curvature.

The trivial bundle B × F has zero curvature and a global section; the Möbius strip is the simplest nontrivial line bundle over S¹ with structure group Z/2; the Hopf fibration S³ -> S² with fiber S¹ is the prototype for SU(2) gauge theory.

title: Der Kult der statistischen Signifikanz — very simple
category_reason: German 'very simple' explanation of the Ziliak & McCloskey critique of p-value worship in empirical economics: why the binary significant/not-significant framework (p < 0.05) distorts scientific inference. Pure statistics / research methodology, no AI content.
thesis: A deliberately simple German-language explanation of why the 'cult of statistical significance' — the practice of treating p < 0.05 as a binary gate for what counts as a real effect — is harmful to empirical science, following the critique of Ziliak & McCloskey (2008/2009), with intuitive analogies and simple numerical examples.
key_claims: A p-value is the probability of seeing data at least as extreme as what was observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true — it is NOT the probability that the null hypothesis is true, nor the probability that the result is a fluke.
The 0.05 threshold is arbitrary (chosen by Fisher as a convenient convention, not a logical boundary); effects with p = 0.049 are not 'real' while effects with p = 0.051 are not 'fake'.

Binary significance testing discards the magnitude of the effect and the strength of the evidence: a p-value of 0.04 with a tiny effect size is published, while a p-value of 0.06 with a large, important effect is ignored.

The correct question is not 'is the effect statistically significant?' but 'how large is the effect, and how precise is our estimate?' — confidence intervals and effect sizes convey more information than p-values.
The 'very simple' framing targets a non-specialist audience (students, journalists, policy makers) who encounter p-values in news reports and need to understand what they do and do not tell them.

title: Was das Froschauge dem Froschhirn sagt — Lettvin et al. 1959
category_reason: German explanation of the classic Lettvin, Maturana, McCulloch & Pitts (1959) paper on the frog's retina: electrophysiological identification of four types of retinal ganglion cells as 'feature detectors' (spot-on, spot-off, edge, moving-edge). thesis: A German-language explanation of the landmark 1959 paper by Lettvin, Maturana, McCulloch & Pitts: by recording from single retinal ganglion cells in the frog, they identified four cell types tuned to specific visual features (bright spot, dark spot, edge, moving edge), arguing that the frog's visual system is optimized for detecting flying-insect prey — a foundational result in computational neuroscience.
key_claims: The frog's retina contains four distinct types of retinal ganglion cells, each tuned to a different visual stimulus: 'spot-on' (bright blob), 'spot-off' (dark blob), 'edge' (light-dark boundary), and 'moving-edge' (directional motion).

The 'moving-edge' detector is the most behaviorally important: it fires only when a dark object moves against a bright background in a specific direction, which is exactly the signature of a flying insect against the sky.

The frog's visual system is not a general-purpose image processor but a highly specialized 'bug detector': the four cell types are sufficient for the frog's ecological niche (catching flying insects) and are not needed for tasks like reading or navigation.

The paper is a landmark in 'functional anatomy': it shows that the brain can be understood as a collection of specialized detectors, each solving a sub-problem, and that the overall behavior emerges from the combination of these detectors.

The McCulloch-Pitts neuron (a binary threshold unit) provides the theoretical framework: each ganglion cell can be modeled as a weighted sum of its inputs (from photoreceptors and bipolar cells) passed through a threshold, making the retina a 'wiring diagram' that can be analyzed logically.

internal_tensions: The paper's 'four cell types' framing is an oversimplification: the frog's retina actually has more than four ganglion cell types, and the 'feature detector' interpretation has been refined by subsequent work; the page presents the 1959 result as the definitive picture.

The 'bug detector' interpretation is ecological but somewhat reductive: the same circuitry is used for other behaviors (startle response, orientation), and the four types are not the only information the frog's brain receives about the visual world.

title: J-Space & Jacobian Lens — Transformer Interpretability
category_reason: German interactive explanation of J-Space (a geometric structure for transformer representation space) and the Jacobian Lens (a tool for reading out intermediate computations), using Temml for embedding visualizations and Plotly for projections. thesis: A German-language interactive explanation of two complementary tools for understanding transformer internals: J-Space, which posits that the representation space of a transformer has a geometric structure (a 'J-space') where semantically related concepts occupy nearby regions, and the Jacobian Lens, which uses the Jacobian of the output with respect to an intermediate layer to read out what the layer is 'thinking' — visualized with Temml embedding projections and Plotly scatter plots.
key_claims: J-Space is the hypothesis that the high-dimensional representation space of a transformer is not a flat vector space but has intrinsic geometric structure: semantically related tokens are close, and the 'distance' between concepts in J-space corresponds to their functional relationship in the model's computation.

The Jacobian Lens works as follows: for a given intermediate layer ℓ and output token v, the Jacobian entry ∂logit(v)/∂h_ℓ[i] measures how much the i-th dimension of the layer-ℓ residual stream influences the probability of token v; this gives a 'lens' that maps the layer-ℓ state to a vocabulary distribution.

Unlike the standard logit lens (which uses the unembedding matrix W_U directly), the Jacobian Lens accounts for the nonlinear transformations in later layers, giving a more accurate 'readout' of intermediate computations at deeper layers.

In J-Space, linear directions correspond to semantic features (e.g., 'positive sentiment', 'past tense'); the geometry of J-space is anisotropic — some directions are 'longer' (more important) than others, and the metric is learned, not Euclidean.

The combination of J-space geometry and the Jacobian Lens allows the user to 'navigate' the model's internal computation: pick a layer, pick a direction in J-space, and see which tokens are affected — a kind of 'X-ray' of the transformer's reasoning.

The Jacobian Lens is computationally expensive (requires backpropagating through all later layers for each token), which limits its practical use to small models or a subset of tokens; the page does not emphasize this computational cost.

title: Sein und Zeit — Interaktive Einführung
category_reason: German interactive introduction to Heidegger's 'Being and Time' (1927): Dasein, being-in-the-world, authenticity vs. inauthenticity, temporality as the horizon of Being. Pure phenomenological philosophy, no AI/ML content.
thesis: A German-language interactive introduction to Heidegger's 'Sein und Zeit': the question of the meaning of Being (Seinsfrage) is approached through the analysis of Dasein (the being for whom Being is an issue), whose fundamental structure is being-in-the-world (In-der-Welt-sein) — not a subject inside a container of objects, but an engaged, practical involvement with equipment (Zuhandenheit) that only breaks down in the moment of concern (Sorge).
key_claims: The 'Seinsfrage' (question of Being) asks not 'what is?' (which is answered by ontology/categorization) but 'what does it mean to be?' — the meaning of Being is temporality (Zeitlichkeit).

Dasein is the being that we ourselves are; its defining feature is that it is 'being-its-Own-most-Possibility' (seine eigentümste Möglichkeit) — it is always ahead of itself, already in a world, and being-alongside entities.

The primary way Dasein encounters entities is not theoretical observation but practical use (Zuhandenheit, 'readiness-to-hand'): the hammer is encountered as 'for hammering', not as an object with properties; the theoretical attitude (Vorhandenheit, 'presence-at-hand') is a derived mode.

Dasein is normally 'fallen' (verfallen) into the They (das Man): it interprets itself through public, average interpretations rather than its own authentic possibilities; authenticity (Eigentlichkeit) requires facing one's own Being-towards-death (Sein-zum-Tode).

Temporality is not clock-time but the ecstatical-horizonal structure of care (Sorge): Dasein is always already projected into the future (Sein-vor-zu), factually situated in the past (Geworfenheit, 'thrownness'), and present in the moment (Geworfenheit in der Gegenwart). The 'circle of temporality' (temporal circle) is the structure in which past, present, and future are not sequential but co-constitutive.

internal_tensions: The interactive format (sliders, toggles) is somewhat at odds with Heidegger's insistence that Dasein's structure must be 'lived' and cannot be reduced to a diagram; the visualizations risk making the existential structures look like mechanical parts.

The page presents 'Sein und Zeit' as a finished system, but Heidegger himself later (in the 'turn', Kehre) distanced himself from the work, and the interpretation of Dasein's temporality remains contested among Heidegger scholars.

title: Universeller Approximationssatz — Interaktive Erklärung
category_reason: German interactive explanation of the Universal Approximation Theorem (Cybenko 1989, Hornik 1991): single-hidden-layer neural networks with suitable activation functions can approximate any continuous function on a compact set, with a constructive proof using bump functions and a Dense-ReLU-Dense architecture. Core neural network theory.
thesis: A German-language interactive explanation of the Universal Approximation Theorem: a single hidden layer with a finite number of neurons and a non-polynomial activation function can approximate any continuous function on a compact subset of R^n to arbitrary precision; the page gives a constructive proof for the 1D case using bump functions (bump = smooth, compactly supported) and shows how a Dense-ReLU-Dense network can be built from them, with Temml-based visualizations of the approximation converging as width increases.
key_claims: Cybenko (1989) / Hornik (1991): for any continuous f: [a,b] -> R and any ε > 0, there exist weights w_i, v_i, c_i and a finite number N of neurons such that |f(x) − Σᵢ vᵢ σ(wᵢx + cᵢ)| < ε for all x ∈ [a,b], where σ is a non-polynomial activation (e.g., sigmoid, ReLU).

The theorem is existential, not constructive: it guarantees the existence of a network that works but does not tell you how to find the weights; in practice, training (gradient descent) is the algorithm for finding them.

A constructive 1D proof using bump functions: any continuous function on [a,b] can be approximated by a sum of scaled and translated 'bump' functions (smooth, compactly supported); each bump can be implemented by a small ReLU network (a 'ReLU bump' = difference of two ReLUs), so the sum is a single-layer ReLU network.

The width of the network (number of hidden neurons) must grow as ε shrinks; there is no bound on the required width in terms of ε alone (it depends on the complexity of f), but the theorem guarantees that a finite width always suffices.

Depth can reduce width: a deep network (many layers, few neurons per layer) can approximate some functions with exponentially fewer total parameters than a wide shallow network, but the UAT only guarantees the existence of a wide shallow solution.

bump functions: smooth, compactly supported functions as building blocks
ReLU as a 'hinge' function: max(0, x) and its use to construct triangular bumps
Dense-ReLU-Dense architecture: y = W₂ ReLU(W₁x + b₁) + b₂
uniform approximation: sup-norm convergence on [a,b]
non-polynomial activation requirement (polynomial activations cannot approximate all continuous functions)

width vs. error plot: a log-log plot of approximation error vs. number of neurons, showing the rate of convergence for different target functions (smooth vs. discontinuous)

internal_tensions: The theorem is for a single hidden layer, but the visualizations use ReLU networks which require a specific construction (difference of ReLUs for bumps) that is not the same as the standard Dense-ReLU-Dense architecture used in practice; the gap between the constructive proof and the practical architecture is not fully bridged.

The theorem says 'any continuous function' but the rate of convergence can be extremely slow for functions with sharp features; the page shows this with the width-vs-error plot but the interactive approximation can be misleadingly fast for smooth functions, giving the impression that the theorem is 'useful' in a practical sense.

title: Modelltheorie — Interaktive Einführung
category_reason: German interactive introduction to model theory (a branch of mathematical logic): structures, languages, satisfaction, elementary equivalence, compactness, completeness, and the Löwenheim-Skolem theorems. Pure mathematical logic with no AI/ML content.
thesis: A German-language interactive introduction to model theory: the branch of mathematical logic that studies the relationship between formal languages (sentences built from symbols and rules) and their models (mathematical structures that satisfy those sentences). The key results — compactness, completeness, and Löwenheim-Skolem — are presented as surprising consequences of the limitations of first-order logic, with interactive examples for the user to explore.
key_claims: A structure M = (M, ·, +, 0, 1, ...) interprets the symbols of a language L and assigns them meaning; a sentence φ of L is 'true in M' (M ⊨ φ) if the interpretation makes it so; the theory of M is the set of all sentences true in M.

Two structures are elementarily equivalent (M ≡ N) if they satisfy exactly the same first-order sentences; elementary equivalence is weaker than isomorphism — there are non-isomorphic structures that are elementarily equivalent (e.g., the rationals and the reals are elementarily equivalent as ordered fields, by the completeness theorem + model of Th(Q)).

The compactness theorem: if every finite subset of a set of sentences Σ is satisfiable, then Σ itself is satisfiable; this leads to counterintuitive results such as the existence of non-standard models of arithmetic (with 'infinite' natural numbers) and the existence of an ordered field between the rationals and the reals.

The completeness theorem (Gödel 1930): a sentence is logically valid (true in all structures) if and only if it is provable from the axioms of first-order logic; this is a syntactic/semantic bridge that does not hold for second-order logic.

The Löwenheim-Skolem theorems: if a countable first-order theory has an infinite model, it has a countable model (downward LS) and a model of every infinite cardinality (upward LS); this means first-order logic cannot pin down the cardinality of a structure, even for the natural numbers.

The page presents model theory as a self-contained branch of logic, but its applications (e.g., to database query optimization, program verification, and the foundations of physics) are not mentioned, which may make the subject seem purely abstract to a practical reader.

title: Analytischer Idealismus — Interaktive Erklärung
category_reason: German interactive explanation of Bernardo Kastrup's analytic idealism (based on his 2019 Radboud University dissertation): a consciousness-only ontology where phenomenal consciousness is the sole ontological primitive, matter is the extrinsic appearance of transpersonal consciousness, and individual minds are dissociated 'alters' of a universal consciousness. Philosophy of mind, no AI/ML content.
thesis: A German-language interactive explanation of Kastrup's analytic idealism: the only thing that exists is universal phenomenal consciousness; the physical world is the extrinsic (third-person) appearance of transpersonal consciousness activity; individual organisms are dissociated 'alters' of this universal consciousness (analogous to alters in dissociative identity disorder); and the correlation between brain activity and experience is explained not by causation but by the brain being the extrinsic appearance of the experience itself.
key_claims: Analytic idealism posits a single ontological primitive: universal phenomenal consciousness. There is no 'matter' in the fundamental sense; the physical world is a model (extrinsic appearance) of the activity of consciousness, analogous to how the 'wave' is a model of the activity of the ocean.

Dissociation — a well-documented clinical phenomenon (DID) — explains how a single unified consciousness can give rise to apparently separate subjects: a dissociative boundary separates the 'internal' (subjective) experience of an alter from the 'external' (transpersonal) activity of the whole.

Perception is the experience of transpersonal consciousness activity that has been 'coded and compressed' by the dissociative boundary: external thoughts hitting the boundary are experienced as sensory qualia; the coding is lossy and optimized for fitness (per Hoffman/Friston), not for truth.

The brain-experience correlation is not causal (brain causes experience) but constitutive: the brain is what the experience looks like from the outside (extrinsic perspective); damage to the brain changes the appearance, not the experience itself — which explains why reduced brain activity (hypoxia, psychedelics, NDEs) can be associated with expanded consciousness.

Analytic idealism avoids both the hard problem (no need to explain how matter gives rise to experience, since there is no matter) and the combination problem of panpsychism (no need to explain how micro-experiences combine, since there is only one macro-experience that is dissociated).

internal_tensions: The page presents Kastrup's ontology as if it were empirically supported, but the 'evidence' section (hypoxia, psychedelics, NDEs) is anecdotal and the correlation between reduced brain activity and expanded experience does not uniquely support idealism — it could also be explained by changes in the brain's filtering/gating mechanisms under physicalism.

The dissociation analogy (DID) is powerful but risky: DID is a trauma response, and equating the structure of a trauma disorder with the fundamental ontology of the universe is a large inferential leap that the page does not adequately qualify.

The quantum field analogy (field -> particles via self-excitation) is used for intuition but is physically inaccurate: particles in QFT are excitations of a field, not 'self-excitations' in the sense the page implies; the analogy is suggestive but should not be taken literally.
